entries.register: neutral, but tied to transport; formal or ceremonial outside it
entries.complement: noun phrase only — a vehicle or vessel. No gerunds, no clauses, no ordinary places: aboard the terminal is wrong. It is also a bare adverb with no object at all (All aboard!, Welcome aboard), which is the usual test for telling the two uses apart
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] aboard [vessel / vehicle] · [verb] [object] aboard [vessel / vehicle] · aboard [vessel / vehicle], [main clause]
entries.contrast: Aboard covers both the motion and the resulting position, so it does the work of onto and on at once — but only for craft. Everyday American English says get on the plane; climb aboard the plane is the heightened or official register (announcements, journalism, nautical writing). The spelling trap: the figurative "in agreement" sense is two words — get everyone on board with the plan, never onboard or aboard — while onboard as one word is an adjective for equipment (onboard navigation).
entries.meaning: The vessel preposition. It began as sailors' vocabulary and spread to trains, buses, planes, and spacecraft, keeping its slightly formal flavor the whole way. Its figurative use — joining a crew, and so joining a company or a project — is now common in business English, but almost always as the adverb (welcome aboard) rather than with an object. Senses: 1. Motion onto a vessel or vehicle. 2. Position on a vessel or vehicle. 3. Joining a crew, staff, or undertaking (figurative).
examples: We climbed aboard the trawler before sunrise.
They loaded the horses aboard the transport one at a time.
Everyone aboard the train felt the jolt.
The instruments aboard the probe are still returning data.
Two of the three crew members aboard the vessel were rescued.
He came aboard the firm as a junior partner.
She brought two of her old analysts aboard the project with her.
Compare the two-word idiom: we need the union on board before we announce anything.

entries.ipa: /əˈɡɛnst/, also /əˈɡeɪnst/, casual /əˈɡɛns/ with the final t dropped before a consonant
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (advised against going) — never a finite clause. Write against the idea that he was lying, not against he was lying
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] against [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] against [noun phrase] · against [verb-ing] · stranded: the wall he threw it against
entries.contrast: Against is the contact-with-force preposition; on and onto are neutral about force. Put the ladder on the wall is odd; lean it against the wall is right, because against supplies the pressure. For a target you aim at but may miss, use at — threw a rock at the window (aim) vs. threw a rock against the window (it landed).
entries.meaning: Motion that terminates in forcible contact, or motion that pushes back on an opposing force. The static "leaning" sense is really the resting state left behind by that motion, which is why the same word covers both. From there the meaning generalizes to opposition of every kind — political, legal, and physical — and finally to a backdrop, where one thing is seen pressed up against another. Senses: 1. Motion ending in forcible contact. 2. Resting contact under pressure. 3. Motion opposing a force. 4. Opposition, hostility, competition. 5. Seen with something behind it. 6. Protection or insurance from.
examples: The rain beat against the windshield the whole way home.
He kicked the ball against the garage door until his mother made him stop.
She leaned her shoulder against the doorframe and waited.
Two rakes stood against the shed.
Walking against that wind was like walking uphill.
The salmon fight their way against the current for miles.
Every senator from the state voted against the bill.
Her lawyer advised against saying anything publicly.
The lighthouse showed white against the storm clouds.
His accent stood out against everyone else's.
The clinic vaccinates against four strains.
We're insured against flood but not against fire.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only. With a clause it stops being a preposition and becomes a conjunction (as far as I know, as far as anyone can tell) — a different construction with a different meaning
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] as far as [noun phrase] · [measurement] as far as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: As far as marks the far end of a distance actually covered; up to marks a ceiling that may not be reached (up to fifty people means fifty at most). We walked as far as the bridge says the bridge is where we stopped. Note also the disputed truncation as far as money, we're fine — standard edited English wants as far as money is concerned or simply as for money.
entries.meaning: Names the limit of a movement or an extent: the point where the walking, the driving, or the seeing stops. The literal spatial sense extends easily to abstract reach (as far as the evidence goes). Beware the clause version, which is a completely different animal: as far as I know hedges a statement and has nothing to do with distance. Senses: 1. The farthest point of a motion. 2. The limit of an extent or a view. 3. The limit of an abstract reach.
examples: She walked as far as the mailbox and had to sit down.
The bus goes as far as Ninth Street, then loops back.
Corn as far as the eye could see.
The flood reached as far as the second step.
His authority runs as far as the state line.
The grant covers tuition, but only as far as the first two years.

entries.ipa: /əˈtɑp/, also /əˈtɔp/ in the regions where the cot–caught merger settles on the rounded vowel — the same variation you hear in on, onto, and upon. The vowel is the one in top, so speakers who keep the two apart use /ɑ/ here
entries.register: neutral to formal; commonest in journalism, sports writing, and physical description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses of any kind. It is one of the most restricted prepositions in this file: it wants a concrete object that has a top. Unlike aboard, around, and along, it has no bare adverb use — he stood atop with nothing after it is not English
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] atop [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] atop [noun phrase] · [noun] atop [noun phrase] (the flag atop the dome) · sit / perch / sit atop [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Atop is onto and on compressed into one word with a summit added: it asserts that the object has a high point and that the thing is at it. A book on the table is neutral; a book atop the table is faintly odd, because a table's top is not a summit. Reserve it for things with a real high point — a hill, a roof, a pole, a stack, a standings table. Against upon: both are raised in register, but upon is about contact and atop is about height.
variants: on top of — the ordinary spoken equivalent and the safer choice in plain prose; see the complex prepositions file. The older a-top of is obsolete.
entries.meaning: The summit preposition. It was built the same way as aboard and ashore — a worn-down on fused to a noun — and it does in one word what on top of does in three, which is exactly why headline writers and sportswriters reach for it. Its figurative life is almost entirely about rankings and hierarchies: a team sits atop the standings, an executive sits atop an organization. Senses: 1. Position on the top of. 2. Motion to the top of. 3. Highest in a ranking or a hierarchy (figurative). 4. Piled on; added to what is already there.
examples: A wind sock hung atop the pole at the end of the runway.
Snow was still sitting atop the ridge in June.
She climbed atop the stepladder to reach the smoke detector.
The cat hauled itself atop the refrigerator and stayed there all afternoon.
They finished the week atop the conference for the first time since 2011.
He spent twelve years atop the agency before anyone questioned the budget.
A second rate hike atop the one in March would break the deal.
The fee sits atop everything else the school already charges.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (back to working nights) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] back to [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] back to [noun phrase] · back to [verb-ing] · dates back to [year]
entries.contrast: Plain to is neutral about whether you have been there before; back to asserts you have. Go to Denver is a trip; go back to Denver is a return. Do not confuse the temporal sense (dates back to 1890) with since, which measures forward from a start point rather than reaching backward from now.
entries.meaning: Return motion — to a place, a state, an activity, or a point in the past. The back carries all the "again" meaning; to supplies the destination. In its temporal sense it reaches from the present into the past, which is why it pairs with date, go, trace, and reach. Senses: 1. Return to a place. 2. Return to a state or condition. 3. Return to an activity or topic. 4. Reaching into the past.
examples: We drove back to the hotel in the dark.
He moved back to Ohio after the divorce.
The swelling went back to normal overnight.
After the layoffs, nothing went back to the way it was.
She went back to teaching after ten years in software.
Getting back to your question — no, we haven't decided.
The family's records go back to the 1830s.
The feud traces back to an argument over a fence.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (came down to choosing between two) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] down to [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] down to [noun phrase] · everything down to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Directional down to mirrors up to and, like it, has an "as far as and including" sense — but down to the last detail scans the list from big to small, while up to fifty counts from zero to a ceiling. The British sense "attributable to" (it's down to you, that's down to the weather) is not American; Americans say up to you for responsibility and because of or due to for cause.
entries.meaning: Motion to a lower place, a farther-along point, or a smaller amount. The "lower" is often social or geographic rather than literal — Americans go down to the city, down to Florida, and down to the store without any change in elevation. Senses: 1. Motion to a lower or farther point. 2. Reduction to a level. 3. As far as and including the smallest item.
examples: He went down to the basement to reset the breaker.
They drove down to Austin for the weekend.
The doctor got her dosage down to five milligrams.
We cut the guest list down to forty.
The set is period-accurate down to the light switches.
Everything was accounted for down to the last penny.

entries.ipa: /ˌɑn ˈrut tu/, also /ˌɛn ˈrut tu/, weak /ˌɑn ˈrut tə/. The route here is /rut/ ROOT, never the American /raʊt/ ROWT
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in travel, shipping, aviation, and news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — a destination or an outcome. A gerund is idiomatic in the figurative "on the way to achieving" sense that sportswriting made common (en route to winning her third title), but never a finite clause: en route to he arrived is not English. Strip the to and bare en route is an adverb with no object at all (the parts are en route), which is the test for telling the two uses apart
entries.pattern: [be / verb of motion] en route to [destination] · [clause], en route to [destination] · en route to [verb-ing] (figurative)
entries.contrast: En route to insists that the trip has started and has not finished, which is what separates it from plain to and from toward: flying to Denver reports the whole trip, en route to Denver reports only the part in progress. Against via: via names the waypoint and en route to names the destination not yet reached, so the two sit at opposite ends of the same journey and often appear in one sentence (en route to Santa Fe via Amarillo).
variants: enroute — the closed spelling is common in aviation and military writing and is still treated as an error in edited American prose. Keep the two words.
entries.meaning: The in-transit preposition. English already owns to, toward, and on the way to, but none of them states as flatly that the motion is under way, which is why dispatchers, airlines, and delivery notifications run on this one. Sportswriting then borrowed it for a figurative sense — the points a player scores en route to a win are the ones scored along the way — and that use is now at least as common in American print as the literal one. Senses: 1. In transit to a destination. 2. Stopping or passing through, on the way somewhere else. 3. On the way to an outcome or an achievement (figurative).
examples: The ambulance was en route to the hospital when the call was canceled.
Your package is en route to the sorting facility in Memphis.
Two of the crates were damaged en route to the warehouse.
The delegation stopped in Reykjavik en route to Brussels.
We refueled twice en route to the coast.
He threw for four touchdowns en route to a 38–10 win.
She set a personal best en route to winning her third state title.
The bill picked up nine amendments en route to the governor's desk.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə dəˈrɛkʃən əv/, weak /ɪn ðə dəˈrɛkʃən ə/ — the final of reduces to a bare schwa in every ordinary use, exactly as in out of and off of. Both /dəˈrɛkʃən/ and /daɪˈrɛkʃən/ are standard American, and the unstressed /də-/ is the commoner one inside this phrase
entries.register: neutral, but four syllables longer than the word it replaces; in political and official prose it is usually a hedge
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — the object belongs to the final of. It also takes a nominal wh-clause (in the direction of where the shots came from), which is a noun phrase in disguise; it never takes a that-clause. A gerund is grammatical but graceless (a move in the direction of settling) — write toward settling
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] in the direction of [noun phrase] · point / gesture / nod / look / turn in the direction of [noun phrase] · a step / a move in the direction of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is toward in four words, and toward is nearly always the better choice. The phrase earns its length in exactly two places: when the direction is being indicated rather than traveled (he nodded in the direction of the door — he did not move, so toward would mislead), and when a writer wants to name a bearing without claiming a destination (a move in the direction of reform promises less than a move toward reform). Against as far as: that names a limit actually reached; this names a bearing only. If toward fits, use toward.
entries.meaning: The long form of toward, useful mainly for pointing rather than going. Because it names a bearing and commits to nothing else, it is also the standard hedge in official and political language — nobody who calls a policy a step in the direction of something has promised to arrive. Learners meet it constantly in reading and should recognize it on sight, but should reach for the one-word preposition when writing. Senses: 1. Moving on a bearing toward something. 2. Pointing, looking, or gesturing toward, with no motion of the pointer. 3. Partial or hedged progress toward a goal (figurative).
examples: The herd moved slowly in the direction of the river.
He drove off in the direction of the interstate without saying where he was going.
Rescuers headed in the direction of where the last signal came from.
She tipped her chin in the direction of the man by the window.
The trooper pointed in the direction of the exit ramp.
Everyone in the diner turned in the direction of the noise.
The settlement is a small step in the direction of real oversight.
Nothing in the budget moves in the direction of the reforms they promised.

entries.complement: whatever the following to takes — a noun phrase or objective pronoun when to is a preposition (turned it in to the clerk), or a bare verb when to is the infinitive marker (came in to talk). Never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb + in] to [noun phrase] · [verb + in] to [bare verb] · [verb] [object] in to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The mirror image of on to, and the test is the same. If "to a position inside" fits, write into as one word. If in belongs to the verb — turn in, hand in, drop in, come in, stop in, check in, log in, give in, cave in, tune in, sit in, call in — the words stay apart. He turned himself in to the police means he surrendered; he turned himself into the police means he became them.
entries.meaning: Not a preposition, but the counterpart the onto / on to pair makes everyone expect — and the error it prevents is funnier and commoner than its sibling's. Two distinct things hide behind the same two words: to as a real preposition after a particle verb (hand it in to the office) and to as an infinitive marker of purpose (stopped in to say hello). Neither can ever be spelled into.
examples: She turned the paperwork in to the registrar on Friday.
He dropped in to see how the remodel was going.
Log in to the payroll site with your employee number.
They finally gave in to the union's last demand.
I'll come in to sign the forms tomorrow morning.
Turn your keys in to the front desk when you check out.
Compare: she walked into the registrar's office.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (got into arguing about it), or a wh-clause in the inquiry sense (an investigation into what went wrong, look into how this happened) — never a that-clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] into [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] into [noun phrase] · into [wh-clause] · stranded: the room she walked into; what did you get yourself into?
entries.contrast: in is position, into is motion — He was in the pool vs. He jumped into the pool. This is the central contrast of the whole file. Separately, write in to as two words when in belongs to the verb: turned himself in to the police (he surrendered), came in to talk, dropped in to say hi. Turned himself into the police would mean he became them.
entries.meaning: The general preposition of entry — motion from outside to inside, with the boundary crossed. From there it fans out into some of the widest polysemy in English: collision (where the "inside" is contact), transformation (where the thing enters a new state), penetration into a time span, inquiry, division, and the informal enthusiasm sense. Senses: 1. Motion to a position inside. 2. Motion ending in collision. 3. Change of state or form. 4. Penetration into a period or a distance. 5. Inquiry, investigation. 6. Enthusiasm for (informal). 7. Chance encounter (with run, bump). 8. Division (arithmetic).
examples: Pour the batter into the pan and level it off.
The dog bolted into the woods and didn't come back for an hour.
She backed into a pole in the parking garage.
He walked straight into the screen door.
Translate the whole thing into Spanish by Friday.
The argument turned into a shouting match.
We were three weeks into the semester before anyone noticed.
They kept rehearsing into the early morning.
The board opened an investigation into the missing funds.
I'll look into what happened with your order.
He's been into woodworking since he retired.
She's not into horror movies at all.
I ran into my old landlord at the hardware store.
We bumped into each other outside the courthouse.
Four into twenty goes five times.
Divide the class into groups of three.

entries.complement: whatever to takes — noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (moved on to fixing the roof) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb + on] to [noun phrase] · hold on to [noun phrase] · pass [object] on to [noun phrase] · move on to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The whole entry exists for one test. If you can substitute "to a position on top of," write onto as one word. If on belongs to the verb — hold on, move on, pass on, hang on, sign on, log on, catch on — keep the two words apart. He held on to the rail (he gripped it) vs. He climbed onto the rail (he got up on it). Log on to the server, not log onto the server.
entries.meaning: Not a preposition, but the single most useful non-entry in this file: American writers get onto and on to wrong constantly, and the error is always in the same direction — collapsing a particle verb into a false preposition. Read the sentence with on attached to the verb; if it still makes sense, the words stay apart. One genuine gray area: be on to someone ("have discovered what they're doing") is written both ways in edited American prose, with onto now slightly commoner.
examples: Hold on to the handrail — those steps are slick.
Let's move on to the second item.
She passed the message on to her supervisor.
Log on to the portal with your employee ID.
Hang on to that receipt in case it doesn't fit.
He signed on to the project in March.
Compare: she stepped onto the platform.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. Gerunds are marginal — onto winning is not idiomatic. Never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] onto [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] onto [noun phrase] · stranded: the ledge he climbed onto
entries.contrast: on is position, onto is motion — The cat was on the roof vs. The cat jumped onto the roof. And see on to for the two-word spelling: use onto only where "to a position on top of" fits.
entries.meaning: The surface counterpart of into: motion that ends with the moving thing resting on a surface. The extension to data and media (copy it onto a drive) treats the destination as a surface, and the informal "aware of" sense treats a person's scheme as something you have climbed on top of. Senses: 1. Motion to a position on a surface. 2. Transfer onto a surface or medium. 3. Emergence onto an open space. 4. Aware of, having caught on to (informal).
examples: She stepped onto the platform just as the doors closed.
The cat leapt onto the counter the second we left.
Load the boxes onto the truck first.
He transferred the tape onto his laptop.
Their balcony looks onto the parking lot.
The kitchen door opens onto the alley.
I think she's onto something with that theory.
Don't bother lying — they've been onto you for weeks.

entries.ipa: /tɔrd/ (the normal American one-syllable form), also /təˈwɔrd/, /ˈtoʊərd/. The one-syllable /tɔrd/ is itself the reduced form — it is what Americans say in ordinary connected speech, and the two-syllable /təˈwɔrd/ is the careful or emphatic pronunciation, not the other way around. The -s of towards does not change any of this
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (a step toward solving it) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] toward [noun phrase] · [noun] toward [noun phrase] (his attitude toward the job) · toward [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: to arrives; toward only aims. She ran to the door means she got there; she ran toward the door leaves it open. That is the whole difference and it is reliable. Against at: threw it at me is aggressive and targeted, threw it toward me is merely directional.
variants: towards — identical in meaning. American English strongly prefers toward; towards is the dominant British form. Both are correct in the United States; pick one and be consistent within a document. The same -s alternation runs through forward(s), backward(s), upward(s), afterward(s).
entries.meaning: Direction without commitment to arrival — which makes it the preposition of aim, orientation, approach, and partial progress. Its abstract senses all preserve that logic: an attitude toward something faces it, money toward a purchase moves you closer without completing it, and toward evening approaches evening without being it. Senses: 1. Motion in the direction of. 2. Facing or orientation. 3. Approaching a point in time. 4. Attitude or feeling directed at. 5. Contributing to a goal.
examples: The herd drifted toward the far fence.
We rowed toward the lights on shore.
He tilted the lamp toward the page.
All the seats face toward the stage.
It usually clouds over toward evening.
Toward the end of the book she loses the thread.
Her policy toward latecomers is not forgiving.
Public opinion has shifted toward the proposal.
That's a real step toward fixing the problem.
Half his paycheck went toward the loan.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses
entries.pattern: [verb] unto [noun phrase] · [noun] unto [noun phrase] (a law unto himself)
entries.contrast: In every living use, unto is a stylistically marked substitute for to. Using it in ordinary modern prose reads as either scriptural pastiche or unintentional comedy — the sole exceptions are the three fixed phrases below.
entries.meaning: The King James Bible preserved unto long after ordinary English dropped it, which is why it survives almost entirely in quotation and in a handful of frozen idioms. It is worth knowing because Americans encounter it constantly in hymns, oaths, older legal boilerplate, and the phrases a law unto himself and do unto others. Senses: 1. To (motion or recipient) — archaic. 2. Until, up to the point of — archaic. 3. Fixed modern idioms.
examples: "Suffer the little children to come unto me."
He rendered unto the county what the county was owed.
She stayed loyal unto the very end.
They swore to defend it unto the last man.
The coach is a law unto himself and the athletic director knows it.
Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (not up to driving tonight); a wh-clause only in the "someone's choice" sense with extraposition (it's up to you how we split it). Never a bare that-clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] up to [noun phrase] · up to [number] · be up to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · it's up to [pronoun] · stranded: what are you up to?
entries.contrast: Up to names a ceiling that may not be reached (up to fifty people = fifty at most, possibly fewer); as far as names a limit actually reached. Against down to: both mean "as far as and including," but up to counts upward from nothing and down to scans from large to small.
entries.meaning: Motion as far as a point — and then, by an easy extension, a maximum, a standard, a capability, and an obligation. The "doing something (usually shady)" sense is one of the most idiomatic constructions in casual American English and has no literal spatial content left in it. Senses: 1. Motion as far as a point. 2. A maximum. 3. As far as and including a time. 4. Capable of, feeling well enough for. 5. Doing something, usually mischief. 6. Someone's decision or responsibility. 7. Meeting a standard.
examples: A stranger came up to me outside the station.
He drove up to the gate and rolled down the window.
The theater seats up to four hundred.
Delivery takes up to ten business days.
Up to that point the meeting had gone fine.
She'd been sober up to the wedding.
I'm not up to going out tonight.
Is he really up to the job?
The kids have been suspiciously quiet — they're up to something.
What have you been up to since graduation?
Whether we appeal is up to the client.
It's up to you where we eat.
The inspector said the deck isn't up to code.
His second album wasn't up to the first.

entries.ipa: /əˈpɑn/, also /əˈpɔn/. The first syllable is already reduced and there is no further weak form: it is /ə/, never the full /ʌp/ of up, and UP-on is the commonest mispronunciation among learners who see the spelling before they hear the word
entries.register: formal, literary, or fixed-phrase; in plain modern prose on is the default
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (upon signing the contract) — never a finite clause. The gerund pattern is the one place upon beats on in modern American writing
entries.pattern: [verb] upon [noun phrase] · Upon [noun phrase / verb-ing], [main clause] · [noun] upon [same noun] (row upon row)
entries.contrast: Upon and on mean the same thing; upon is longer, heavier, and more formal. Reaching for it to sound elegant is the classic overcorrection — sit upon the couch is simply worse than sit on the couch. Reserve it for the four places it earns its keep: after certain verbs (depend upon, call upon, seize upon), in the temporal upon + gerund, in the doubling pattern (row upon row), and in frozen phrases (once upon a time).
entries.meaning: The elevated twin of on, and — in its motion sense — a near-synonym of onto with a sudden or forceful edge: things fall upon, descend upon, and come upon one another. Its most genuinely useful modern job is temporal: upon arrival and upon signing compress a whole clause into two words, which is why contracts and instructions are full of it. Senses: 1. On a surface (formal). 2. Motion onto, often sudden. 3. Immediately after (with a noun or gerund). 4. Chance encounter (with come, happen, stumble). 5. Doubling for quantity.
examples: A heavy snow lay upon the fields.
The inscription upon the stone had worn away.
Winter descended upon the valley all at once.
The crowd surged upon the barricades.
Upon signing, you'll receive a copy of the agreement.
Upon hearing the verdict, she left without a word.
I happened upon the letter while cleaning out the attic.
They stumbled upon the wreck by accident.
Mile upon mile of the same brown grass.
Thousands upon thousands of people showed up.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (moving away from using coal) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] away from [noun phrase] · [measurement] away from [noun phrase] (two blocks away from the station) · away from [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Plain from names the origin of a trip (flew from Denver); away from stresses increasing distance and often avoidance (flew away from the storm). Against out of: out of requires an enclosure to exit, away from does not — you move away from a tree, never out of one.
entries.meaning: The direct opposite of toward: motion whose whole point is that the gap is widening. It also does static duty as a distance measurement, and it carries a strong secondary sense of deliberate avoidance, which is why warnings use it (stay away from the edge). Senses: 1. Motion increasing distance. 2. Distance measured from a point (static). 3. Abstract shift or change of course. 4. Avoidance.
examples: He backed slowly away from the dog.
The plane banked away from the ridge.
The cabin is four miles away from the nearest road.
They live two doors away from my parents.
The company is shifting away from hardware entirely.
She's been drifting away from her old friends.
Keep the kids away from the fireworks.
I'd stay away from that restaurant if I were you.

entries.ipa: /ɔf/, also /ɑf/ for speakers with the cot–caught merger. No weak form — off keeps its full vowel even when unstressed, which is why off of reduces in its second word (offa /ˈɔfə/) and never in its first
entries.register: neutral; the "obtain from a person" sense is informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund only in the "sustained by" sense (lives off selling parts). Never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] off [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] off [noun phrase] · stranded: the shelf it fell off
entries.contrast: Off is the surface counterpart of out of: you get off a bus, a plane, a horse, or a roof (you were on it), but out of a car or a taxi (you were in it). Against from: bought it off a guy is informal for bought it from a guy — the from version is what edited prose wants. See off of for the two-word variant.
entries.meaning: Separation from a surface, and by extension from a route, a habit, or a supply. It is also one of the busiest verb particles in English (take off, call off, put off, knock it off), and the object test is the only way to tell the two apart: He took his hat off the hook has an object for off; The plane took off does not. Senses: 1. Motion away from and losing contact with a surface. 2. Removal from a surface. 3. Leaving a route; branching from. 4. Situated at a distance from a coast or a road (static). 5. No longer using or consuming. 6. Sustained by; drawing income from. 7. Obtaining from a person (informal — prefer from).
examples: The mug slid off the counter and shattered.
He fell off the ladder but landed on the grass.
Wipe the frost off the windshield before you back out.
She pulled the tag off the mattress.
Their driveway comes off the county road.
The exit ramp off the interstate is closed.
There's a sandbar half a mile off the beach.
He rents a studio just off Sixth Avenue.
The doctor took him off the blood thinner.
She's off sugar until the wedding.
The whole cabin runs off a single solar panel.
He got through college living off selling his prints.
I bought the truck off a guy in Reno.
She borrowed the ladder off her neighbor.

entries.register: informal — normal in American speech, widely edited out of formal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] off of [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] off of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Semantically identical to off; the of adds nothing. Style guides and copy editors delete it on sight, and Get off of the couch becomes Get off the couch with no loss. It is far commoner in American English than in British English, so American speakers often do not notice it. In speech it is unremarkable; in edited prose, cut it.
entries.meaning: The redundant doublet of off. Worth an entry only because learners hear it constantly from native speakers and reasonably conclude it is standard — it is standard speech, not standard writing. Every sentence below is ordinary spoken American English, and every one of them improves in print by deleting the of.
examples: Get your feet off of the coffee table.
He jumped off of the diving board without looking.
She wiped the mud off of her boots.
Take that sticker off of the window.
The paint is peeling off of the porch railing.
I got the recipe off of my grandmother.

entries.ipa: /aʊt/, with the final t flapped to /ɾ/ before a vowel (out an open window /ˌaʊɾ ən/) — the same reduction that turns out of into outta
entries.register: neutral; the "along" sense is informal and regional
entries.complement: noun phrase only, and only a narrow set of them — openings and routes (the window, the door, the driveway, the highway). It cannot take a gerund or a clause, and it cannot take most ordinary nouns: out the building is wrong; you need out of
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] out [opening] · [verb] [object] out [opening]
entries.contrast: As a true preposition, bare out is almost entirely restricted to openings — out the window, out the door, out the back. Everywhere else the preposition is out of. Note the transatlantic split: Americans say threw it out the window; British speakers prefer out of the window. Elsewhere out is an adverb (go out, the lights are out), an adjective, a noun, and a verb.
entries.meaning: Chiefly an adverb and a particle; a preposition only in the opening construction, where it names the aperture the motion passes through. American English has extended it informally to routes (drive out the highway), which sounds regional to many ears and should be avoided in writing. Senses: 1. Through and beyond an opening. 2. Along and away, of a road (informal, regional).
examples: He tossed the cigarette out the car window.
The cat slipped out the back door before anyone noticed.
Smoke was pouring out the vents.
She watched the parade go by out the front window.
Keep going out the county road until you see the silo.
They live out Route 12, past the grain elevator.

entries.ipa: /ˌaʊt frəm ˈʌndər/ — the stress lands on under, and from is always the weak /frəm/, never the full /frʌm/; casual /ˌaʊt frəm ˈʌnɚ/ with the d dropped after the nasal
entries.register: neutral; the figurative "free of a burden" sense is the commoner one in American writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — the object belongs to under. No gerunds, no clauses of any kind: write out from under the mortgage, never out from under he owed money. Unlike out and under on their own, the stack has no bare adverb use — he finally got out from under with nothing after it is heard in speech but leaves the object to be understood, not deleted
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] out from under [noun phrase] · get / dig / climb / crawl / haul out from under [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] out from under [noun phrase] · be out from under [burden]
entries.contrast: Each of the three words does a job, which is why nothing shorter replaces it: under names the starting position, from marks it as a source, and out says the exit was completed. Out of the porch is wrong (you were never inside it), and from under the porch loses the sense of having gotten clear. Against out of: out of needs an enclosure, out from under needs only something on top. Against off: off leaves a surface you were on, out from under leaves a weight you were beneath.
entries.meaning: One of the few genuinely productive preposition stacks left in English, and American English treats it as a single unit. The literal sense is the exit of something covered or pinned — a cat out from under a parked truck, a foot out from under a fallen beam. The figurative sense generalizes the weight to anything that presses down: a debt, a boss, a contract, a verdict. Senses: 1. Motion out of a position beneath something. 2. Pulling something out of a position beneath something else. 3. Freed from a weight, a debt, or an authority (figurative).
examples: The cat shot out from under the parked truck when the engine started.
She wriggled out from under the collapsed shelving without a scratch.
He backed the mower out from under the deck stairs.
Somebody yanked the rug out from under the whole argument.
Two more payments and they'll be out from under the second mortgage.
The division never got out from under the last reorganization.
It took a decade to climb out from under that verdict.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (talked me out of quitting) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] out of [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] out of [noun phrase] · out of [verb-ing] · [number] out of [number] · stranded: the mess we got out of
entries.contrast: Out of is the exit counterpart of into, just as off is the exit counterpart of onto: you get out of a car (you were in it) but off a bus (you were on it). Against from: from names an origin without an enclosure (a letter from Ohio), out of requires something to come out of (a letter out of the file).
entries.meaning: The general preposition of exit — and then, through the metaphor of a container, the preposition of source, material, motive, depletion, and proportion. The depletion sense (out of milk) is so common that it has almost broken free of the spatial one, but the logic still holds: the supply is a container and you have come to the end of it. Senses: 1. Motion from inside to outside. 2. Material or source. 3. Motive or cause. 4. No longer having; depleted. 5. Beyond a range or limit. 6. Proportion; a score. 7. Based in; operating from (characteristically American).
examples: He dragged the mower out of the shed.
Water was seeping out of a crack in the foundation.
The whole cabinet is built out of reclaimed oak.
She quoted a line out of the middle of the report.
I only went out of curiosity.
They stayed together out of habit.
We're out of printer paper again.
He's been out of work since the plant closed.
Keep the knife out of reach of the kids.
The signal drops as soon as you're out of the valley.
She got eighty-eight out of a hundred.
Four out of five respondents said the same thing.
The band is out of Muscle Shoals, not Nashville.
He flies out of O'Hare almost every week.

entries.ipa: /əˈkrɔs/, also /əˈkrɑs/. No separate weak form — the first syllable is already the reduced /ə/ and the stress never leaves -cross, which is true of the whole a- family here (aboard, atop, along, alongside, astride, athwart, around). The regional form acrost /əˈkrɔst/ is nonstandard
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. It is also a bare adverb with no object at all (we paddled across, go across at Fifth), which is the usual test for telling the two uses apart
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] across [noun phrase] · [noun] across [noun phrase] (the diner across the street) · stranded: the river we swam across
entries.contrast: The three-way traversal contrast is the one to memorize. Across is a two-dimensional surface, side to side (swam across the river); through is a three-dimensional medium you are inside of (waded through the river); over is above an obstacle, or across a raised surface (jumped over the puddle, drove over the bridge). All three can describe the same river; they describe different trips.
entries.meaning: Motion from one edge of a surface to the opposite edge. Once the crossing is complete, the same word names the resulting position (the diner across the street), and once you stop thinking of a single line, it names distribution over a whole area (offices across the country). Across has the usual second life outside this word class: an adverb with no object (she waved and ran across) and a verb particle in two very common phrasal verbs, come across (encounter, or make an impression) and get across (communicate). The object test settles which is which — swam across the river has an object and is the preposition, swam across to the far bank has none and is the adverb, and in the point never got across the word belongs to the verb. Senses: 1. Motion from one side to the other. 2. On the opposite side of (static). 3. Distributed over an area. 4. Crosswise; forming a cross.
examples: She ran across the field to catch up.
We drove across three states in a day.
He lives across the hall from me.
There's a bakery across the square.
The company has offices across the country.
Reaction was mixed across the department.
A fallen pine lay across the driveway.
She drew a line across the page.

entries.ipa: /əˈlɔŋ/, also /əˈlɑŋ/. No separate weak form — like across, the first syllable is already /ə/ and cannot reduce further
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only. It requires a linear object — a road, a river, a wall, a coast, a fence. Along the room is wrong; across the room is right
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] along [linear noun phrase] · [noun] along [linear noun phrase] · stranded: the road we walked along
entries.contrast: Across cuts a surface at right angles to its length; along follows the length. Against down and up: all three can describe walking a street, but along is neutral about direction while up and down pick one. Do not confuse the preposition with the complex preposition along with, which means "in addition to" and has no spatial sense.
entries.meaning: Motion that follows the length of something linear, or position strung out over that length. Because it needs a line to follow, it is the natural preposition for roads, rivers, shorelines, fences, and walls, and it is wrong with an area. It is also a heavily used adverb and particle (come along, bring it along, play along, get along), where it takes no object at all. Senses: 1. Following the length of something. 2. Positioned in a line beside something. 3. Following an abstract line of thought or development.
examples: She jogged along the canal every morning.
The train runs along the river for twenty miles.
We drove along the coast road until the pavement gave out.
There are streetlights along the whole stretch.
Wildflowers grow along the fence line.
Sandbags were stacked along the levee for half a mile.
He wants something along the lines of what we did last year.
The reforms proceeded along familiar lines.

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun, and a gerund in the "in addition to" sense (alongside running the shop, she does the books) — never a finite clause. Write alongside the claim that he lied, never alongside he lied. It is also a bare adverb with no object at all (the tug came alongside, she stayed alongside the whole way), which is the usual test for telling the two uses apart
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] alongside [noun phrase] · [noun] alongside [noun phrase] · work / serve / fight / run alongside [person] · pull / come alongside [vessel or vehicle] · alongside [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Along follows the length of a line; alongside puts you next to that line, facing the same way. Against beside (a static location preposition): beside is pure position, while alongside keeps the motion and the shared heading of along — she sat beside him is still, the cruiser pulled alongside us is not. Against with for collaboration: worked with the union claims joint action, worked alongside the union claims only proximity and parallel effort, which is precisely why negotiators and press releases reach for it.
variants: alongside of — the redundant two-word form, exactly parallel to off of: unremarkable in speech, deleted in edited prose.
entries.meaning: The nautical word that came ashore. A ship comes alongside a pier — parallel to it, touching or nearly touching — and every later sense keeps that picture: two things side by side, pointed the same way, one of them usually having moved to get there. The collaboration sense is now the commonest one in American writing, and its deliberate weakness compared with with is the whole reason it gets chosen. Senses: 1. Motion to a position beside and parallel. 2. Position beside and parallel (static). 3. Working or serving in parallel with (figurative). 4. In addition to; at the same time as.
examples: A pickup pulled alongside us and honked.
The tug came alongside the barge and made fast.
There's a drainage ditch alongside the whole access road.
They parked the trailer alongside the barn.
He worked alongside his father for twenty years.
Volunteers served alongside the county crews all week.
The rebate runs alongside the existing credit, not instead of it.
Alongside the layoffs, the company cut its travel budget in half.
Alongside teaching two sections, he advises the debate team.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund in the abstract "centered on" sense (built around getting the timing right). Never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] around [noun phrase] · [noun] around [noun phrase] · around [number / time] · stranded: the block we walked around
entries.contrast: Against past: drove around the accident means you took a curving path avoiding it; drove past the accident means you went by in a straight line. Against through: around the crowd skirts it, through the crowd penetrates it. The approximation sense competes with about — both are fine in American English, and around is the commoner spoken choice.
variants: round — the same word with the a- worn off. In American English round as a general preposition is British-sounding (walked round the lake); Americans keep it only in fixed expressions: round the clock, all year round, year-round, come round, round about. Write around unless you are inside one of those phrases.
entries.meaning: One of the most polysemous prepositions in the language, unified by the idea of a curved or enclosing path. From a circular route it moves to enclosure, to skirting an obstacle, to aimless wandering inside an area, and finally — because a circle has no exact edge — to approximation. It is just as busy outside this word class, as an adverb (turn around, stick around, is she around?) and as a verb particle (mess around, shop around, pass it around), and in both of those jobs it takes no object at all. The object test separates them cleanly: we walked around the block is the preposition, with the block as its object, while we walked around for an hour is the adverb, with nothing after it. The same split holds for the variant: come round is the adverb, round the clock is the preposition. Senses: 1. Circular or curving motion. 2. Surrounding position. 3. Motion to the other side of an obstacle. 4. Aimless motion within an area. 5. Approximately (of time, number, amount). 6. Centered on; organized about (abstract).
examples: The trail loops around the lake and comes back.
She wrapped a scarf around her neck.
There's a fence around the whole property.
The kids gathered around the fire pit.
Traffic was routed around the construction.
The bathroom is around the corner on your left.
He spent the afternoon poking around the hardware store.
She showed us around the house.
There were around fifty people at the service.
Let's say around four o'clock.
The curriculum is organized around four themes.
Their whole schedule is built around the baby's naps.

entries.register: neutral to literary; fully everyday only with horses, bikes, fences, and shoulders
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. It also has a bare adverb use in older prose (he rode astride rather than sidesaddle), but the preposition is what you meet in modern American writing, and it always has an object
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] astride [noun phrase] · sit / stand / swing / climb astride [noun phrase] · [noun] astride [noun phrase] (a town astride the border)
entries.contrast: Against athwart, the other crosswise word in this file: athwart lies across something and usually obstructs it, while astride straddles it with a leg — or a half — on each side and obstructs nothing. Against across: a bridge across the river only spans it, but a city astride the river has real substance on both banks. Against on: you ride on a horse in ordinary speech and astride one when the writer wants the posture in the picture.
entries.meaning: The straddling preposition — one leg on each side, and by extension one part on each side. It stays alive in ordinary American English for riding (astride a horse, astride the fence) and in a productive figurative use for anything that sits on both sides of a line: a company astride two industries, a town astride a state border. Senses: 1. Mounted or seated with a leg on each side. 2. Extending across, with part on each side. 3. Occupying both sides of a boundary or a category (figurative).
examples: He climbed astride the fence rail and refused to come down.
The boy sat astride his father's shoulders for the whole parade.
The county road runs astride the ridge for two miles.
Their property lies astride the creek, which is why the survey took so long.
The city is astride the state line and has two of everything.
The company sits astride logistics and retail and answers to regulators in both.

entries.register: literary, nautical, and archaic — rare in ordinary American prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses of any kind
entries.pattern: [verb] athwart [noun phrase] · lie / stand / run athwart [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In its spatial sense it is a heightened across, with an added suggestion of obstruction or of a crosswise angle. In its figurative sense it means "in opposition to," where ordinary prose uses against. Using it unironically outside nautical writing or deliberate rhetoric will read as affectation.
entries.meaning: An old word for "crosswise," surviving chiefly in sailing (athwart the deck, athwartships) and in one famous rhetorical formula — to stand athwart history, yelling Stop. Included here for completeness and because readers meet it in older prose, not because anyone should reach for it. Senses: 1. Across, especially at an angle or as an obstruction. 2. In opposition to (figurative).
examples: A fallen mast lay athwart the bow.
Shadows fell athwart the courtyard.
Storm clouds moved athwart their course.
The decision cuts athwart everything the agency has argued.
He set himself athwart the reform effort from the first day.

entries.ipa: /biˈjɑnd/, weak /bəˈjɑnd/ — the first syllable reduces to a schwa in every unstressed use
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund only in a closed set of "past the point of" idioms (beyond caring, beyond saving, beyond repairing) — you cannot invent new ones. Never a finite clause: write beyond the fact that he was there, never beyond he was there. Beyond is also a bare adverb (the fields beyond) and a noun (the great beyond); as always, the object is the test
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] beyond [noun phrase] · [noun] beyond [noun phrase] · go / stretch / extend / reach beyond [noun phrase] · beyond [verb-ing] (closed set) · far / well beyond [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against past, its plainer twin: both put a line behind you, but past is the ordinary word for the motion (drove past the mill) and beyond is the literary word for what lies on the far side (the country beyond the mill). Against over: over the hill passes above it, beyond the hill is on its far side. Against outside for limits: beyond my control and outside my control both work, with beyond the more emphatic and the more final. This entry covers the spatial and figurative senses only; for the temporal senses — beyond midnight, ran beyond Friday — see beyond in the time file.
entries.meaning: The far-side preposition. Where past reports the crossing, beyond describes the territory on the other side, which is why it leans literary and why so much of its use has gone figurative: a limit, a capacity, an authority, or an understanding is a boundary you can be on the wrong side of, and beyond is the word that puts you there. Senses: 1. On the far side of; farther out than. 2. Motion past and onward. 3. Outside the limit of a capacity, a power, or an authority. 4. Past the point of, in a closed set of idioms. 5. More than; other than (usually under a negative).
examples: There's nothing beyond the last cattle guard but sagebrush.
On a clear day you can see three ranges beyond the valley.
The trail runs beyond the wilderness boundary and keeps climbing.
She walked beyond the last streetlight and then turned back.
The cost is beyond anything we budgeted for.
Whether the permit clears is beyond my authority.
The frame was beyond saving after the second collision.
By the third hour he was beyond caring who was right.
She said nothing beyond her name and her attorney's number.
There's no evidence beyond the one receipt.

entries.ipa: /daʊn/. No weak form — the diphthong keeps its full quality even unstressed, so down is always audible; the same is true of its opposite, up
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. (The look-alike down to does take a gerund; see down to.)
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] down [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] down [noun phrase] · stranded: the hill we rolled down
entries.contrast: Against up: with vertical objects the pair really is opposite (up the ladder / down the ladder), but with streets and hallways both simply mean "along," and the choice is idiomatic or relative to the speaker (down the hall, up the street). Against off: you fall down the stairs (traveling along them) but off the ladder (losing contact with it).
entries.meaning: Motion from a higher point to a lower one along a path — and then, with the vertical sense bleached out, plain motion along a horizontal path. Americans go down the hall, down the street, and down to the store with no change in elevation. Its two figurative senses run in exact parallel with up: an order travels down the chain of command as readily as a complaint works its way up it, and a decision pushed down the road is postponed rather than lowered. It is equally at home as an adverb and particle (sit down, the system is down, turn it down), and there the object test applies: ran down the hill has an object, the car broke down does not. Senses: 1. From higher to lower along something. 2. Along a path (no vertical sense). 3. Following the course of a flow or a coast. 4. Onward through a stretch of time. 5. Lower on a scale, a list, or a chain of authority (figurative).
examples: He slid down the banister.
Water was running down the inside of the wall.
Walk down Third Street until you hit the light.
The copier is down the corridor on the right.
We paddled down the Green for three days.
The fog moved down the coast overnight.
The recipe has come down the family since her great-grandmother.
Down the years the town has barely changed.
We'll worry about the second phase down the road.
Three owners down the line, nobody could find the original deed.
The order came down the chain of command without a signature on it.
Her name slid down the depth chart after the second injury.

entries.ipa: /ˈoʊvər/. No true weak form — the stressed /oʊ/ keeps its full quality however fast you talk, which is why over is always audible where of and to vanish. What does happen is that the second syllable goes syllabic and swallows a following the: over the hill runs together as /ˈoʊvɚðə/
entries.respell: OH-ver, run together as OH-vruh-thuh in over the
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (argued over paying the bill), or a wh-clause in the dispute sense (a fight over who gets the house) — never a that-clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] over [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] over [noun phrase] · over [wh-clause] · stranded: the fence he jumped over
entries.contrast: For traversal, see the three-way rule under across: over implies height — an obstacle cleared or a raised surface crossed. Against above (a static preposition, filed with the location group): above is pure vertical position with no contact and no motion, so a blanket above her knees is impossible, while over allows motion, covering, and contact. On quantity, over thirty people and more than thirty people are both standard American English — the old newsroom ban on quantitative over was dropped by the AP Stylebook in 2014.
entries.meaning: Along with into, the widest-ranging preposition in this file. The core is a curved path passing above something; from there it spreads to covering, to superiority, to exceeding a number, to spanning a period, and to the topic of a dispute — a chain that makes sense once you see that all of them involve one thing positioned above or beyond another. Over also has a heavy second life outside this word class. It is an adverb (come over, move over, the plane flew over), a verb particle (hand over the keys, turn it over, think it over, start over), and a predicate adjective meaning finished (the meeting is over). Two tests separate them. The object test: he climbed over the fence has an object, the fence fell over does not. The movement test for particles: handed over the keys can be split (handed the keys over), while a true preposition can never be pulled away from its object — never climbed the fence over. Senses: 1. Motion above and across. 2. Traversal of a raised or extended surface. 3. Position above, without contact. 4. Covering. 5. More than (number, age, amount). 6. Spanning a period of time. 7. The subject of a dispute or feeling. 8. Authority or control. 9. By means of a medium. 10. Recovered from.
examples: The dog cleared the hedge and kept going over the neighbor's lawn.
A hawk circled over the field.
The trail goes over the ridge and drops into the next valley.
We walked over the footbridge single file.
There's a crack in the plaster right over the door.
Smoke hung over the whole valley.
He spread a tarp over the woodpile.
She put her hands over her ears.
The repair came to over four thousand dollars.
Anyone over sixty-five rides free.
The changes were phased in over six months.
Over the years they'd stopped calling.
The brothers fell out over the will.
There's some disagreement over who signs off on it.
No manager should have that much power over a team that size.
The federal court has jurisdiction over the case.
We settled it over email.
I heard the score over the radio.
She's not over him yet.
Give it a week and you'll be over the worst of it.

entries.ipa: /pæst/, casual /pæs/ with the final t dropped before a consonant (past the store) — one reason the passed misspelling is so persistent
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund in the "beyond the point of" sense (past caring, past worrying about it) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] past [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] past [noun phrase] · [minutes] past [hour] · be past [verb-ing] · stranded: the store we drove past
entries.contrast: The spelling trap: past is the preposition, passed is the past tense of the verb pass. We drove past the school and We passed the school are both correct; We drove passed the school is not. If a form of have or be could precede it, or if it is the main verb, you want passed. Against by: drove by the house and drove past the house are near-identical, with past slightly stronger on the idea of going beyond. Against through and around: past skirts the thing entirely without entering or circling it.
entries.meaning: Motion that goes beyond a point without stopping, and then position beyond that point. The clock sense (quarter past four) is the same beyond-ness applied to time, and the abstract sense — past his prime, past caring — applies it to a limit or a capacity. Past is unusually busy outside this word class: an adjective (past events, the past-due balance), a noun (in the past, she has a past), and an adverb with no object at all (a truck rumbled past). The object test matters more here than almost anywhere else in the file, because the adverb and the preposition sit in the same slot after the same verbs: she walked past the diner has an object and is the preposition; she walked past without looking up has none and is the adverb. The adverb is also the form stranded at the end of a relative clause (the store we drove past), where the object has moved to the front rather than disappeared. Senses: 1. Beyond a point, in motion. 2. Beyond a point, in position. 3. Later than the hour, on a clock. 4. Beyond a limit, an age, or a capacity.
examples: A cruiser went past the window with its lights off.
He shoved past us to get to the door.
The trailhead is a quarter mile past the bridge.
Their place is just past the grain silo.
The meeting started at half past two.
It was already twenty past by the time she called.
Honestly, I'm past caring what he thinks.
The car is well past the point of being worth fixing.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (got through cleaning the garage) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] through [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] through [noun phrase] · [day] through [day] · stranded: the tunnel we came through
entries.contrast: See the three-way traversal rule under across: through means you were inside the thing. Also note a distinctively American use: inclusive through in date ranges — Monday through Friday includes Friday. British English does not use it this way and says Monday to Friday or up to and including Friday, which is why May through September can confuse an international reader. Against by for means: found it through a friend (the friend was the channel) vs. written by a friend (the friend was the agent).
variants: thru — a respelling, not a separate word. It is acceptable only in signage and trade names (drive-thru, thruway) and in informal notes; in any edited prose it is an error.
entries.meaning: Motion entering one side of a volume and exiting the other, or moving within a medium. Everything else follows from that: a period of time is a stretch you pass through, a process is something you come out the far side of, and an intermediary is what your action travels through. The inclusive date sense is one of the few places where American and British usage genuinely diverge in meaning rather than style. Outside this word class, through is an adverb (let me through, the bullet went straight through), a verb particle (the deal fell through, read it through, see it through, follow through), and — in sense 6 — a predicate adjective (we're through, are you through?). The object test applies as usual: we drove through the tunnel has an object, the call didn't go through does not. Senses: 1. In one side and out the other. 2. Moving within a medium or a mass. 3. From beginning to end of a period or process. 4. By means of; via an intermediary. 5. Up to and including (dates — American). 6. Finished with (informal, predicative).
examples: We walked through the tunnel with a flashlight.
Rain was coming through a gap in the roof.
She waded through knee-deep water to reach the truck.
The plow cut through two feet of drift.
He sat through three hours of testimony.
They got through the audit without a single finding.
The grant came through the state, not the city.
You learn that kind of thing through experience.
The pool is open Memorial Day through Labor Day.
Applications are accepted Monday through Thursday.
I'm through with the whole argument.
Let me know when you're through with the car.

entries.ipa: /θruˈaʊt/, weak /θrəˈaʊt/ — the stress sits on the second syllable, so the first reduces in connected speech
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. It needs an object with extent: a space, a period, or a group. Throughout the box is odd; throughout the building is right
entries.pattern: [verb] throughout [noun phrase of space or time] · Throughout [noun phrase], [main clause]
entries.contrast: Through traces a path from one end to the other; throughout saturates every part with no path implied. The smoke went through the house describes a route; smoke spread throughout the house describes total coverage. Against during: during the war locates an event inside a period, throughout the war insists it lasted the whole of it.
entries.meaning: Complete penetration of a space, a period, or a population — "in every part of," never "along a route." Its two senses, spatial and temporal, are the same idea applied to extent in space and extent in time. It also works as an adverb with no object (the house was rewired throughout), which is the usual test for separating the two. Senses: 1. In or to every part of a space. 2. For the whole of a period. 3. Among every part of a group or a body of work.
examples: Speakers were installed throughout the building.
The blight has turned up throughout the county.
He stayed calm throughout the interview.
Throughout the 1970s the plant ran three shifts.
The error appears throughout the dataset.
Support for the measure was strong throughout the district.

entries.ipa: /ˈʌndər/, casual /ˈʌnɚ/ with the d dropped after the nasal in rapid speech (under the bed)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. Write under the assumption that he'd agree, never under he'd agree
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] under [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] under [noun phrase] · under [number] · stranded: the bed it rolled under
entries.contrast: Under is the everyday word and the only one of the four that comfortably takes motion (swam under the bridge). Below is about level on a scale or a vertical position, often at a distance (below sea level, the apartment below). Beneath is under with a formal or literary register, plus the figurative "unworthy of" sense (beneath contempt). Underneath stresses being covered or hidden and is often an adverb (the note was underneath). Against over: they are a true opposite pair across most of their senses.
entries.meaning: Motion to or position in a place lower than something, usually with the upper thing covering or spanning it. The abstract senses all preserve a sense of being subordinate to something above: less than a number, subject to an authority, or in the middle of a process that is being applied to you. Under is also a bare adverb with no object (the swimmer went under, the business went under) and a productive prefix (underpaid, understaffed, underestimate). It is only a marginal verb particle, though — unlike up, down, over, off, and out, it does not build many phrasal verbs — so the preposition is what you meet nearly every time: the ball rolled under the couch has an object, the ship rolled and went under does not. Senses: 1. Motion to a position beneath. 2. Position beneath. 3. Covered by. 4. Less than (number, age, amount). 5. Subject to an authority, a rule, or a condition. 6. In the process of. 7. Filed or classified as.
examples: She ducked under the low doorway.
The kayak slid under the footbridge.
There's a box of photos under the stairs.
The keys were under a stack of mail.
The car sat all winter under a tarp.
Half the driveway was under snow.
Kids under twelve get in free.
He ran it in under four hours.
He testified under oath.
Under the new rules, that's no longer allowed.
The proposal is still under review.
Two of the exhibits are under construction.
File the receipts under "travel."
Her earlier books were published under a pen name.

entries.ipa: /ʌp/. No weak form — the vowel is already lax and does not reduce further, which is why in up to only the second word weakens (UP-tuh, never uh-TOO)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. (The look-alike up to does take a gerund; see up to.)
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] up [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] up [noun phrase] · stranded: the hill we ran up
entries.contrast: The mirror of down, with the same caveat: with vertical objects the two are genuine opposites (up the ladder / down the ladder), but with streets and hallways both mean "along," and Americans use them almost interchangeably (up the street, down the street). Do not confuse the preposition with the particle: ran up the hill (preposition — the hill is the object) vs. ran up a huge bill (particle — run up is the verb).
entries.meaning: Motion from a lower point to a higher one along a path, or simply motion along a path with the vertical sense worn away. In American usage up also carries a directional charge from regional geography — up north, up the coast, upstate — that has more to do with maps than with elevation. As an adverb and particle it is one of the most frequent words in English (wake up, give up, look it up, use it up), and there it takes no object. Senses: 1. From lower to higher along something. 2. Along a path (no vertical sense). 3. Against a current; upstream. 4. Toward the far, northern, or inland end of an extended area. 5. Higher on a scale, a list, or a hierarchy (figurative).
examples: She carried the boxes up the stairs two at a time.
Ivy had grown up the whole north wall.
Go up Fourth Street and take a left at the diner.
The restrooms are up the hall past the elevators.
We poled the boat up the creek as far as it would go.
The barges work their way up the Mississippi in convoys.
Their cabin is about an hour up the lake from the landing.
Everything up the coast from Newport was fogged in.
Word of the defect finally worked its way up the org chart.
She moved up the waiting list after two people dropped out.

entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in travel, logistics, and technical writing
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Gerunds (via emailing him) are awkward and better rewritten (by emailing him). Never a clause
entries.pattern: [motion or transmission] via [place / route] · [action] via [medium or intermediary]
entries.contrast: Via names an intermediate point or a channel, never an origin or a destination — flew from Denver to Rome via Frankfurt has all three, and swapping via into either end position breaks the sentence. Against by for means: by is the ordinary word (by car, by mail), via is heavier and suggests a routed path. Against through: interchangeable for intermediaries (through a friend / via a friend), with via the more clinical choice. The full form by way of means the same and lives in the complex prepositions file.
entries.meaning: The route preposition: it marks the waypoint between a start and a finish. Its second sense, a channel of transmission, is now the commoner one in everyday American writing — email, text, and courier all travel via something. Senses: 1. By way of a route or a stopping point. 2. By means of a channel, medium, or intermediary.
examples: The train runs to Sacramento via Stockton.
They shipped it via Memphis to save two days.
Confirm your appointment via the patient portal.
I got the news via my sister-in-law.
The virus spreads via contaminated water.
Payment can be made via check or wire transfer.
